div.p: Systems with timing constraints have become pervasive in several disciplines, such as real-time articial intelligence, operating systems, operations research, and local area networks. Most of the work in real-time system scheduling deals with admission control algorithms to guarantee that accepted tasks will meet their deadlines. In this paper, we compare the di erent algorithms, and suggest a novel algorithm that subsumes the previous ones with respect to schedulability in the case where the system may su er from transient overloads and where tasks have precedence c onstraints among them. We show how our algorithm works in allocating time to competing reasoning modules in dynamic environments.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Several disciplines using embedded computer control systems rely on applications containing tasks with timing and precedence constraints. Examples of these systems are automated industrial control and autonomous vehicle systems, as well as internet and household appliances. In many dynamic real-time systems, a mechanism is needed to allocate time to competing processes that contend for resources such as CPU time. One speci c example that arises in Arti cial Intelligence AI, is in Moss e w as supported by NSF grant CCR-9308886 y Pollack is also with the Intelligent Systems Program. Ron en and Pollack w ere supported by the Air Force O ce of Scienti c Research Contracts F49620-91-C-0005and F49620-92-J-0422, by the Rome Laboratory RL of the Air Force Material Command and the Advanced Research Projects Agency Contract F30602-93-C-0038, and by an NSF Young Investigator's Award IRI-9258392.
z Work by Ronen done while at the University o f Pittsburgh.

the design of intelligent autonomous agents or the management of teams of cooperating agents. These agents typically have to reason about the location of other agents and how to collaborate or avoid the other agents.

The problem of appropriately allocating the computational resources to an agent who is situated in a dynamic environment is not completely new. It bears a strong similarity to the problems of process scheduling in real-time operating systems ZRS87 , job scheduling in operations research Pin95 , and transmission scheduling in local area networks NT87 . In each case, sets of tasks require resources, and the value of each task is a function of the amount of time a task receives and the time at which a task completes. A wide variety of algorithms for process, job, and transmission scheduling exist e.g., LL73, J L T85, NT87, MP93, ZRS87 , and in this paper we consider whether any of these algorithms can be applied to the deliberation scheduling problem. Our focus is on comparing known schedulability results and improving them for our speci c problem.

Our interest in deliberation scheduling is based on a view of processes that are situated in dynamic and unpredictable environments, which pose a large number of deliberation possibilities. The process needs some mechanism for focusing its attention, deciding which reasoning tasks to perform when, and for how long. Not all processor job-or transmission-scheduling algorithms hereafter, called simply scheduling algorithms" are applicable to this context. In particular, we require scheduling algorithms that a construct schedules dynamically i.e., during run time, consequently supporting dynamic arrival of tasks; b are stochastic, that is, support tasks with random computation times; and c allow for soft real-time scheduling, allowing the tasks to be completed after their deadlines, while still yielding some less than maximal value to the system.

Simple scheduling algorithms for hard real-time systems incorporate deadline information in their schemes and only allow in the system as many tasks as will complete before their deadlines AB90, SBS95, JLT85 e.g., Rate Monotonic, Earliest Deadline First EDF and Least Slack First LSF. The typical metric used to measure performance in these systems is the number or percentage of jobs that nish within their deadlines. It is known that, for a schedulable set of processes, i.e., one for which there exists an schedule where all deadlines can be met, EDF and LSF produce a schedule that meets all deadlines, and hence performs optimally Bak741 . H o wever, the performance of these algorithms degrades sharply when the system is overloaded, i.e., it has to deal with a non-schedulable set of tasks2 .

In SBS95 , Buttazzo et al. presented a comparative study of di erent s c heduling algorithms, concentrating on the system performance during overload situations. They showed that EDF performs best if an admission control is used along with a reclaiming mechanism." This results con rms the work done by Jensen et al. JLT85 see Section 2. The deliberation scheduling problem we study ts this model perfectly, since it is impossible to predict whether there will or will not be an overload at one time or another.

In dynamic systems, to schedule overloaded job sets e ectively, s c heduling algorithms must take i n to account the tasks' timing constraints as well as the cost of missing a deadline. To e v aluate the importance of a task, value density of a job J has been de ned as the value to the system of completing job J divided by its remaining computation time. Value-density assessments are included in scheduling algorithms such as Best-E ort BE and Dynamic-priority DP; previous research has shown that these algorithms perform better than EDF and LSF in overloaded environments JLT85, NT87 .

The goal of this paper is twofold: rst, to explore the usefulness for real-world applications of deliberation scheduling based on the value-density measure; second to devise an algorithm that performs better than the existing ones. Towards this end, we h a ve so far identi ed appropriate candidate algorithms Section 2, conducted experiments to compare the performance of these algorithms Section 3, and demonstrated a proof-of-concept use of these algorithms for deliberation scheduling in the DIPART system Section 4.1. We h a ve also analyzed the limitations of the current algorithms and suggested a new algorithm BE-v that encompasses the advantages of the value-density and admission control algorithms, and deals positively with their limitations.

div.head: Value-density Algorithms
div.p: Finding an optimalschedule for a non-schedulable set of tasks is a hard problem Pin95 . Allowing for the value of each task to be de ned as a function of its completion time adds to each task another characteristic called a time-dependent utility function or time-value function. This forces the use of heuristics instead of exhaustive searches.

In this section we brie y review three key scheduling algorithms, all of which make use of a valuedensity-like metric: the Best-e ort algorithm BE JLT85, Loc86 , the Simpli ed-rolling-horizon-N wtrule SRHW algorithm MP93 , and the Dynamicpriority DP algorithm NT87 . These algorithms all satisfy the three criteria mentioned above, while performing well under transient o verloads.

We assume that each job J i may h a ve m phases, ph 1 i ; :::; ph m i , such that ph j i cannot start before ph j,1 i ends. Each J i can be characterized as ha i ; c i ; d i ; v i i, where a i is the arrival time of job J i , c i is its worst case execution time, d i its deadline the time after which the value to the system starts diminishing monotonically, v i is the maximal value of completing J i . Note that no value will be accrued from the completion of an individual phase, unless all m phases of a job complete.

div.head: Best-e ort Scheduling
div.p: Best-e ort BE scheduling JLT85, Loc86 , the rst algorithm developed speci cally for scheduling tasks in soft-real-time systems, is based on the following two theorems: 1. Given a set of processes with known computation times and deadlines that can be met, EDF will meet all deadlines LL73 .

2. If deadlines are ignored and processes have known values for their completion, then a sequence of processes in decreasing order of value density will produce a total value at every process completion time at least as high as any other sequence JLT85 .

div.head: BE ALGORITHM
div.p: Let Q be the current job set, containing all jobs currently available to the scheduler i.e., all jobs that have arrival time less than or equal to the current time, and that have neither completed nor aborted. Then: 1. Schedule Q according to EDF 2. While Q is overloaded, do: a Find the rst job in Q whose deadline will necessarily be missed; call it Q i b Remove a minimal value-density job that precedes Q i The BE algorithm combines these two results by using an EDF approach whenever the current job set is schedulable i.e., underloaded, and by incorporating value densities to restore an overloaded state to an underloaded one by load shedding. The BE algorithm is summarized in Figure 2.1. BE has been shown to outperform alternative s c heduling algorithms e.g., EDF, highest-value-density-rst, and FIFO for all utility functions during overloads JLT85, Loc86 .

div.head: Simpli ed Rolling Horizon Scheduling
div.p: A closely related scheduling algorithm is the Simpli ed-rolling-horizon-N wt -rule SRHW MP93 . A job is said to be tardy if its expected completion time is after its deadline. The system's idle time is the amount of time during which no jobs are available for execution. The partial makespan is the sum of all processing times of jobs plus all idle time, both up to the rst tardy job. Using these definitions, we can describe SRHW as follows. If there is a tardy job in the queue, remove the job with the smallest v j =p jk , where v j is the current v alue of job j, and p jk is the reduction in partial makespan if j is removed. The close similarity b e t ween BE and SRHW should be clear.

div.head: Dynamic-Priority S c heduling
div.p: The dynamic priority DP scheduling algorithm was developed, which, like BE and SRHW, is based o n a v alue-density calculation NT87 . In DP, each task i.e., message to be transmitted has an associated cost, which is a function of the time of transmission. This cost function is the inverse of the time-value function de ned for the task. Therefore, at a certain time namely, the message deadline a message to be transmitted starts accumulating a cost, which rises directly to its maximum in a hard deadline situation, and as a di erentiable function in a soft deadline situation.

Unlike the BE algorithm, DP does not determine whether its current job set is schedulable. To o set this lack of global knowledge, DP utilizes stronger measures of job-speci c information,namely urgency and dynamic priority. T o determine the urgency of a message, DP integrates the message's future cost, thus taking into account sharp rises ahead. The dynamic priority o f a n y task is then computed by dividing urgency by the remaining transmission time. Dynamic priority i s t h us related to value density, except that it takes into account both the current v alue of some task and a measure of the rate of change of that value.

In NT87 , the following closed-form solution for computing the dynamic-priority, P i t, for rampshaped utility functions is presented. Let v i be the value to the system of completing job i, X i t and rct i t be the urgency and remaining computation time of task i at time t, a i be the arrival time of job i, c 0 i be the instantaneous cost rate at time t, and be a discounting factor.

Also jobs with small slack are scheduled similarly to value density. The discounting factor is problematic because there is a di erent optimal value for for di erent situations. A large has the e ect of biasing the DP towards value density-like s c heduling whereas a small increases the e ect of slack time on the DP, and thus produces a bias towards LSF-like s c heduling. Nassehi and Tobagi NT87 suggest using a value for equal to the average computation time, a suggestion we adopt in our experiments.

div.head: Simulation Results
div.p: Possibly because BE and DP were developed in di erent areas of computing, they had not, to our knowledge, been directly compared 3 . W e conducted two t ypes of experiments: in the rst, we aimed to show that the experiments with widely varying parameters and distributions thereof would con rm that value density algorithms would perform similarly to EDF in non-overloaded environments, and better in overloaded ones. For completeness we also considered FIFO in these experiments, and veri ed it performed poorly when compared to the valuedensity algorithms. Our second experiments focussed on a direct comparison of the value-density BE and DP algorithms.

The main parameters manipulated were: Average load in the system. For each trial, the load was held constant at one of the following values: 0.8, 0.9, 1.2, and 1.7. Job value, computation time, and arrival distributions. We experimented with exponential, gaussian and uniform distributions. possibility of job preemption. Jobs were only preempted by the arrival of a new job. scheduling algorithm FIFO, EDF, BE, DP number of phases of a job: 1, 5, or 10. = c i for DP's as suggested in NT87 . Each experiment consisted of 1000 jobs and each combination was run 100 times. The results presented below are the average over the 100 trials. With this length of experiments, the results are statistically signi cant as follows: in Table 1, all di erences greater than or equal to 2 were signi cant t o the 0.05 level or less P 0.05; in Table 2, all differences greater than or equal to 3 also had P 0.05; in Table 3, all di erences greater than or equal to 5 had P 0.02; and in Table 4, all di erences greater than or equal to 2 had P 0.01.

Tables 1 and2 give the results of the rst set of experiments: the former shows percent of maximum score obtained by each algorithm as a function of the system load and arrival time distribution. Score is de ned as the sum of the values that would be accrued by the system if all jobs submitted were to be completed. Clearly, this is an upper bound on the value of the system. In both experiments the slack time was constant, the decay function was a 45-degree linear function, and all jobs had a single phase. The key results are:

1. EDF outperforms FIFO in all situations. 2. EDF is comparable to value-based schedulers in sometimes-overloaded environments, i.e., average load of 0.8 this is the statistical average, and therefore the system is sometimes overloaded. For load 0.9, value-based schedulers outperform EDF except for an exponential distribution, where all three algorithms perform comparably. 3. In overload situations loads of 1.2 and 1. 1. In multi-phase settings, value density algorithms continued to outperform EDF for loads of 0.9 and higher. 2. The possibility of preemption always led to a better result than if there were no preemptions4 . This result again points to the commitment" that is built-in to the value-density measure: because it already has a bias toward alreadyexecuting jobs, preemption will occur only when it is truly a good thing. As there are more opportunities for preemption, scheduling time increasingly becomes a factor to be considered and disallowing preemption may play an important role. 3. No obvious and consistent advantage could be found for either BE or DP. The only statistically signi cant di erences were where preemption was allowed for single phase jobs see BE and DP were smaller than the di erence between them and EDF FIFO.

div.head: The Application to Deliberation Scheduling
div.p: We studied the potential usefulness of the value-density-based algorithms for the deliberationscheduling problem. For this, we made use of DIPART, the Distributed, Interactive Planner's Assistant for Real-time Transportation planning PZE + 94 . DIPART is a prototype simulation system that includes a network of agents, each of which assists a human planner, and a simulated dynamic environment, which implements a Non-combatant Evacuation Operation NEO scenario RTBH93 . The DIPART platform was designed to support experimental assessment of alternative strategies for distributed, real-time planning PZE + 94 .

div.head: The DIPART simulator
div.p: The DIPART scenario involves a region from which citizens must be evacuated. For this, they must rst be brought b y truck to the region, and then airlifted. Evacuation can be complicated by unexpected road or bridge closings, due to natural disasters or hostile attacks, and it can also be com-plicated by the fact that citizens that must themselves get to major cities before being taken to the capital.

The NEO is to be planned and overseen by several human planners typically, DIPART is run with between 2 and 6 planning nodes. Each planner is responsible for a di erent component of the operation; although the task may be divided into various parts, each planner typically attempts to move one group of citizens to the capital. The exact size and location of the group may be unknown to the planner.

Each h uman planner submits goals to his her DI-PART node for example: evacuate 300 people from City C, using 4 trucks. The human planner also assigns priorities to the goals perhaps City C i s more prone to attacks, therefore this goal should have higher priority than other goals. The DIPART planning node manages multiple goals, with many phases; the node makes a plan, deciding, for example, which trucks and routes to use. The plan is then dispatched for execution in the simulated world. This process can be changing dynamically, when new goals and new information arrive i n t h e system. Each n o d e m a y h a ve only a restricted view of the environment. Because each node performs the role of an intelligent assistant, we sometimes refer to the nodes as agent processes". The internal architecture of each DIPART n o d e is based on a generic model of process scheduling, similar to those found in the literature on operating systems. Each node is message-driven and messages are placed in a message queue; these messages may be generated either internally or externally. Internal messages result when the system's reasoning state changes, for example, when it completes estimation of the resources needed for some goal, and is thus ready to plan for that goal. Examples of externally generated messages include those that specify a new goal submitted by a h uman user, or those that convey information about events in the environment. Often, the value of responding to the message is a time-dependent function. Thus, deliberation scheduling is needed to determine what processes should run in response to each message, and to schedule the selected processes. The scheduling is performed by a component called Locus of Meta-Level Control LMC; the scheduling produces an order of invocations of DIPART's various Reasoning Modules RMs.

div.head: Algorithm Adaptations for DIPART
div.p: The BE and DP algorithms variations are used in DIPART. Goals submitted to DIPART h a ve several phases of processing, and not all information needed for scheduling all phases is available when a goal is received. The xed sequence of phases applied to each goal is: a goal initiation phase, b compu-tation time estimation phase, c planning phase, d resource allocation and plan submission phase, e execution phase, and f the goal scoring phase. When a goal is received, it comes with a deadline and value function. However, the system must infer value, computation time, and deadline information for each phase. The value for each phase depends on the value of the goal, since value is only accrued upon completion of all tasks in the goal.

Computation time is estimated in phase b, when a reasoning module is invoked. The estimator uses domain knowledge about the average speed of the transport vehicles, their capacity, the numb e r o f p e ople to be evacuated and the distances to be traversed to estimate the number of truck trips that will be required. Computation time for planning is approximated and made available by statistically analyzing planning time for certain types of goals taken at run-time from a lookup table and multiplying by the number of truck trips to be planned. Computation time for other phases is approximated, again using prior experience; other phases constitute a small portion of the CPU usage.

A particular problem arises in DIPART i n volves short phases phases b, d, f. Although they are short, requiring small computation times, we h a ve observed that they should be assigned a larger CPU allotment, otherwise their fair share is too easily swallowed up by small uctuations in processor load. In addition, a question arises about the appropriate use of the value-density calculations of these phases.

According to Section 4.2.1, they should be assigned higher priority, but Section 4.2.2 professes that these short teasers5 should be assigned lower priority. W e therefore explored not only the behavior of the BE and DP algorithms, but also variations on them, that we designed to modify the treatment of short teasers.

div.head: EDF-h and BE-h
div.p: In this variation h stands for high priority, the short teasers were given highest priority. This is justi ed since allowing larger CPU allotments for these short phases will not hurt the larger phases too much. This scheme supports our problem in several ways: 1 performing estimations on a new goal as soon as possible would allow better scheduling, thus phase b should get higher priority, 2 after a goal has been fully planned, quickly allocating resources and sending the plan for execution, thus phase d should get higher priority, and 3 a goal that has completed should deallocate its transport vehicles and receive a score as soon as possible, thus phase f should get higher priority. In EDF-h, the short phases are serviced in FIFO order, whereas the long" phases are scheduled by EDF, but strictly after the short phases while still obeying the precedence constraints. BE-h is similarly de ned.

div.head: BE-v
div.p: A second variant BE-v attempts to deal with the inadequacy of BE's value density based strategy for scheduling short teasers. Recall that, in BE, during overloads, the job with the lowest value-density i s removed from the queue. BE-v instead considers removing two alternatives: the lowest value density job lvdj and the lowest value job lvj. If lvdj 6 = lvj and removing lvj would prevent the overload, then it checks whether value,density lvj value,density lvdj expected,utility lvj expected,utility lvdj If this inequality holds, BE-v removes lvdj; otherwise BE-v removes lvj. The intuition follows from the D over KS92 algorithm: to determine which job to abort one must consider not only value densities but also the ratios of the value densities and expected values; the latter is used to determine if a higher value job should be aborted in favor of a higher value density job.

For example, suppose the queue contains two jobs j 1 , j 2 with respective v alues 5, 20, computation times 50, 220, and deadlines of 80, 225 from the present time. This is an overload situation and one job must be aborted. BE would remove j 2 because its value density of 1 11 is less than that the 1 10 of j 1 . If no other jobs arrive before time 225, then the agent w ould have accrued a score of 5 from this scheduling. BE-v on the other hand would remove the shorter job because 11 10 is not greater than 20 5, thereby scoring 20.

div.head: DIPART Results
div.p: This section presents experiments we conducted in DIPART to answer several questions: Are the adaptations discussed in section 4.2 useful? Can simple estimation heuristics provide accurate information to repeat results from the simulations? And if so, what improvements might be made to make the algorithms more suitable for deliberation scheduling?

More concretely, the main hypotheses were: 1. a The two v alue density algorithms BE-h and Be-v perform similarly to each other and b Value-density algorithms BE-h and Be-v perform better than EDF and EDF-h during overloads or underloads. 2. The di erences would be apparent mostly in environments with a high degree of variation in task value because DIPART estimators, communication and scheduling costs, as well as stochastic computation and execution times do not have the nice properties of any distribution studied in the simulations. In addition, we w ere interested in the relative performance of our two v ariations on BE BE-h and BE-v when compared with BE or DP.

Our experiments used a factorial design varying the following parameters: scheduling algorithm one or more of EDF, BE, DP, and their variants, system load 0.8, 1, 1.4, 2, 4, shape of the decay function step decay and exponential decay, amount o f slack equal to the average job computation time and twice that, the distributions types Gaussian for a smaller standard deviation and Exponential for larger standard deviation environment for a variety of parameters, including value and CPU requirements. Data was collected using the CLIPS system, and statistical signi cance was tested with paired Ttests were conducted between all pair combinations within a column unless noted otherwise all data for a column pertains to all the schedulers executing the same data, sche e tests and ANOVAs using CLASP And93 . Our results are summarized in Table 5 and pertain to a base case of exponential value distribution with high standard deviation, exponential people distribution, gaussian truck distribution, gaussian slack distribution with average xed at twice the average computation time, a time ratio such that planning and execution times are of similar duration, and exponential decay utility function. These settings map naturally to a rapidly changing environment for which planning time is signi cant, and in which the deadlines are important, but some tolerance is allowed. Because of the long running times for experiments on DIPART about 1 day for each experiment and the hypothesis that at low loads all the schedulers would perform similarly, results were not obtained for EDF-h and BE-h at load 0.8.
The main DIPART results can be summarized as follows:

1. Hypothesis 1a was, surprisingly, not conrmed: DP fails to perform on a par with BE for loads 1.4 and higher. This is in contrast with the results of the simulator. In fact, in DIPART at higher levels of saturation, DP's performance is similar to that of EDF. This result suggests that DP is scheduling with more emphasis on slack than value density, which m a y be the result of an value that is too small. The value was chosen based on suggestions made by the authors of DP. F or underloaded situations load 0.8 jobs have more slack, and DP performs on a par with all the other algorithms because it schedules jobs similarly to LSF, which is itself equivalent to EDF for underloaded situations as stated previously. 2. Hypothesis 1b is con rmed: for highly overloaded environments loads 2 and 4 BE outperforms EDF, while in rarely overloaded or semi-saturated environment loads 0.8 and 1 re-spectively both algorithms perform similarly. These results suggest that EDF as adapted for DIPART is indeed optimal in environments that are rarely overloaded. The di erence between BE and DP, a s w ell as the di erence between BE and EDF grow as the load increases. As the loads become higher EDF's shortfall of not incorporating value information becomes more prominent.

3. Regarding hypothesis 2: The results in Tab l e 5 h a ve a relatively large standard deviation of 7; in another set of experiments with a smaller standard deviation of 2.5, EDF outperformed BE by a small margin 51.6 to 47.7 , P=0.046 when using the gaussian distribution, and 50.5 to 48.3 , P=0.26 when using the exponential distribution for load. In addition, in this latter set of experiments, EDF completed more goals than BE 53 to 45, P=0.02. When the values of goals approach uniform value, the fact that EDF completes more goals than BE allows it to achieve a similar score overall even in overloaded environments. These observations con rm hypothesis 2.

4. Regarding how our variations performed: BE and EDF signi cantly outperformed their counterpart adaptations BE-h and EDF-h respectively only at load 1, and they performed on a par for higher loads. For load = 1, the high priority s c hemes used in BE-h and EDF-h are not e ective, probably because the motivations for BE-h and EDF-h were outweighed at this load by the disadvantage of not scheduling all computations uniformly based on the active scheduling policy. As the load increased past 1, the strategy of using high priority for short phases proved to perform on a par with other schemes. Further, BE-v scored higher than BE in a semisaturated environment load 1.4 and did not degrade performance at other loads. BE-v does better than BE when there is an abundance of short teasers: in that case, there are spells of overloaded periods followed by underloaded periods. If under these conditions a large job is aborted for a smaller higher-value-density job and no new job arrives after the smaller job completes, there will be wasted CPU.

To summarize, for soft deadlines and overloaded environments BE outperforms EDF when the value distribution is su ciently non-uniform for utility considerations to outweigh number of goals completed; this is what is expected and what we s a w through the simulations. For these settings BE also outperforms DP and the di erences between BE and EDF and between BE and DP grow as the load becomes heavier. EDF-h and BE-h at best lead only to equal performance with BE and EDF. In sometimes overloaded environments for which the abundance of short teasers is greatest load 1.4 for the experiments presented, BE-v outperforms BE and all the other scheduling algorithms tested. For higher or lower loads both BE-v and BE perform similarly.

div.head: Conclusions and Future Research
div.p: In this paper, we h a ve identi ed scheduling algorithms that may be appropriate for a problem such as meta-level deliberation, and compared their performance both in a generic testbed and in a small, intelligent-agent simulation. We discussed certain adaptations that were needed to use the algorithms for deliberation scheduling. We also identi ed the existence of short teasers and examined certain problems that arose from those types of tasks.

Our experiments showed that BE-v scheduling appears to be a promising algorithm for the deliberation scheduling problem, when value, deadline, and computation times are available or can be estimated. This is often the case in well-tested and well-known environments. BE schedulers are based on a heuristic and it is easy" to come up with variations that deal with speci c shortfalls; BE-v adds to BE a heuristic that deals e ectively with short teasers.
